bullets.t: Karnak is the temple of Amun-Ra, king of the gods, in Thebes, modern Luxor. Kings kept building it for about two thousand years, which is why it is a maze rather than one design.
The first firm evidence is a sandstone column of King Intef II, about 2100 BC, naming Amun-Ra. Before that, no temple of Amun seems to have stood here.
Karnak began on a sandy island between Nile channels, and it grew westward as the river moved west. The First Pylon now stands on ground the river gave up.
Most of what you see was added in the New Kingdom, from about 1500 to 1100 BC: obelisks, the Great Hypostyle Hall, pylons. Kings each added to the axis, from the Fourth Pylon outward.
The god was rich. Papyrus Harris I, written for Ramesses III, lists Amun's gifts, and summaries say his temples held most of Egypt's temple land. The priests grew powerful.
About 1348 BC Akhenaten cut Amun's name out of temples and moved to Amarna. His successor Tutankhamun restored the temples, and Horemheb took Akhenaten's temple at Karnak down for fill.
Later came Libyan, Kushite and Assyrian rulers, who sacked Thebes in 664 BC. Then Persians, Ptolemies and Romans. Building stopped, and Christians later used the Akhmenu as a church.
Mariette's Antiquities Service took charge in 1858. Since 1967 French and Egyptian teams, the CFEETK, have studied and restored Karnak. UNESCO listed ancient Thebes in 1979.

intro.note: The end of worship at Karnak is undated in the sources, so the guide says only that it ended in the fourth or fifth century AD.
